title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:26–31)
hook: carrying the cross, he stops to comfort weeping women

segments.voice: Yesterday, release Barabbas, and the voices that prevailed. Your line was three times, no fault. What true thing did you say once more when the room got loud? Day five hundred eighty-five.

A man is coming into the city from the countryside, minding his own business. His name is Simon, and he's from Cyrene, in North Africa. Suddenly soldiers grab him and put a wooden beam on his shoulders, and he's walking behind a condemned man he's never met. That's how Luke starts the road to the cross: with a stranger forced to help. Behind them follows a great crowd of people, and among them, women. They're beating their breasts and wailing, the way people mourned the dead. And then Jesus, who has barely spoken since the courtyard, stops and turns to them.
screen: `SIMON OF CYRENE, PULLED FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the King James words: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Think about where he is. Beaten through the night, mocked by soldiers, now walking to his own execution. Every reason to be wrapped up in his own pain. And he turns to the people grieving for him and thinks about them. He looks ahead to days of suffering coming for that city, when people will call the childless blessed and ask the mountains to fall on them. Then a proverb, hard to translate and harder to pin down: "For if they do these things in a green tree, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood is hard to burn; dry wood catches at once. One common reading goes like this: if this is what's done to an innocent man now, think how much worse it will be when the times are dry. Scholars debate who the they is and exactly what's meant; the saying is short and doesn't explain itself. Many connect his warning to the Roman siege of Jerusalem a generation later. Only Luke tells this scene: women openly mourning him on the road, and Jesus stopping to speak to them. Later it became part of the Stations of the Cross, the devotion where Christians walk the way to Calvary in fourteen stops. Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem is the eighth. On the worst day of his life, he still turns toward someone else's grief.
screen: then, large: `DAUGHTERS OF JERUSALEM, WEEP NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone while you're struggling. Settle, and breathe. Name honestly what's hard for you right now. Let it be real. Then, without pushing it away, think of one person near you who is also carrying something. A friend after a breakup. A coworker with a sick parent. A neighbor who's lonely. Picture one small comfort you could offer them today, even from inside your own hard week. A text. A coffee. Ten minutes of listening. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Calvary. The place of the cross that Jesus walked toward while stopping to speak to the weeping daughters of Jerusalem, now the eighth stop of the Stations of the Cross.
Your line: weep not for me. Today, even if your own week is hard, turn toward one person who's hurting and offer them something small. Day five hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, stopping at the eighth station to remember Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

original.note: Greek: daughters of Jerusalem. a biblical way of addressing the women of the city, found also in the Song of Songs.

trapdoor: what you thought: some women cried as Jesus went by.
what it means: on the way to his death, Jesus turns from his own pain to the grief of the women and the city's future.
what a scholar hears: only Luke has this scene; the green and dry tree proverb is debated; and the scene became the eighth Station of the Cross.

notes: Cyrene in North Africa (modern Libya). Confirm.
Traditional Stations of the Cross: the eighth is Jesus meets the women of Jerusalem. Some newer forms (e.g. the scriptural stations) differ. Confirm.
Interpretations of the green and dry wood proverb vary (who 'they' are; whether the contrast is innocent/guilty or present/future). Presented as debated.
Link to the Roman siege of AD 70 phrased as 'many connect'. Confirm.
'Daughters of Jerusalem' also in the Song of Songs (e.g. 1:5): confirm the original-game note.

Audit (second sample): fixed a garbled 'two things only Luke gives us' (the Stations of the Cross are later devotion, not Luke); softened 'most readers hear'; the closing line no longer calls a warning 'comfort'.
